newsitem.title: ITALY: GOLF-HOLE IN ONE FOR QUIRICI.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-HOLE IN ONE FOR QUIRICI.

text.p: Switzerland's Paolo Quirici holed in one in the third round of the Italian Open on Saturday but his final-hole bogey allowed playing partner Jose Maria Olazabal of Spain to snatch the lead.
Quirici's seven-iron shot into the cup on the 158-yard short second enabled him to wrest top place early on from overnight leader Eduardo Romero of Spain.
But the favoured seven-iron then turned villain on the 18th when a shot with it went into the crowd instead of finding the final green and a dropped shot there let in Olazabal.

Olazabal birdied the last to make up for an untimely double-bogey on the 13th and set up a five-under-par 67 which took him to 10-under- par overall and a one-shot lead over Quirici, who carded 68 for an aggregate nine-under.

Romero recovered from early bogeys with four successive birdies after the turn but a bogey on the 17th meant he had to settle for a 71 and a share of third place with young Britons Steve Webster, Dean Robertson and Raymond Russell and Sweden's Patrik Sjoland. Webster, 22, equalled the course record 65 to come through the field.
Olazabal surged into contention from two strokes off the lead at the start of the day by reaching the turn in two-under-par.
The 31-year-old Spaniard is now a remarkable 69-under-par in 27 rounds of six tournaments since he made his comeback after 18 months out with foot injuries.

He tracked his playing partner Quirici with two birdies after the turn but then drove into trees with one of three errant drives, nearly hitting out of bounds left on the 13th to allow Quirici to put light between them.
An eagle on the long 16th and a second shot to only four feet on the last, though, edged Olazabal ahead.

"My driving has not been good for the last two rounds after a good first day," said Olazabal, looking for his second win in six events after his Turespana Masters victory. "And if I don't get it right for the final round then I won't win because at least 15 players can go past me."

Quirici's delight at his ace, his sixth in his career, was tempered by his finish. "I knew it was in when it was in the air," said the 29-year-old Swiss, who missed much of the last tour year with diabetes problems.
"I've not won anything because the (prize) car is for the 17th par-three. The only time I won anything for a hole in one was when I was an amateur and got an ashtray in Spain!

"The seven iron did me down in the end, though, because I hooked it at the end when I lost concentration. I backed off so many times and hit into the crowd. It's my biggest fault and I have to get it right if I'm to get anything tomorrow."
